It appears that this feature is activated at punctuation marks that serve as “numerical or unit‐boundary” indicators. In context, it flags the end of a number or similar entity so that the model produces the appropriate subsequent token (a numeral, unit label, or related symbol) rather than an unrelated fallback (“vet”).

explanations.explanation: This feature appears to act as a “structured delimiter detector” – it fires when the text is in a non‐standard, formatted context (like dates, URLs, file paths, ratings, model numbers, or other patterned numeric/alphanumeric strings) and causes the model to predict the correct punctuation or separator (e.g. “/”, “.”, or a special symbol) instead of a generic continuation like “the.” Essentially, it signals that the following token comes from a domain‐specific, well‐formatted sequence rather than ordinary prose.

It captures a “follow‐up” or attribution structure—detecting phrases (like “followed,” “headed,” “driven,” etc.) that cue an ensuing prepositional phrase (usually “by …”) to introduce an agent or complementary detail.

explanations.explanation: It’s a signal that a pronoun or similar subject is about to enter a contraction—effectively, a feature that drives the model to produce the appropriate clitic (like ’s or ’ve) for a natural, contracted construction.

It appears that this feature is signaling an upcoming shift in discourse—typically the introduction of a quotation, reported speech, or an elaborative remark. In other words, when the feature is active, the model “knows” to launch into a quoted or highlighted segment (or a content‐rich clause), whereas without it the prediction defaults to a punctuation or different closure.

It appears to be a structural “boundary‐marker” feature: it fires on tokens—often numerals, ordinal markers, or proper name endings—that denote an item’s or section’s identity (as in book numbers, level labels, or name suffixes) and signal a transition or list element in structured text.

It appears that this feature “lights up” exactly when the model is processing a word‐piece that is an incomplete (or leading) portion of a word—that is, it signals that the current token is a subword prefix that needs to be “completed” by the following token. In short, it encodes a word‐fragment or subword‐continuation signal.

It appears that this feature “lights up” when the model is emphasizing a core, evaluative or intensifying element in the text—marking words (and nearby punctuation or symbols) that shift a description from generic information into a more assertive or focused claim.

This feature appears to be signaling that the current word is one that normally sets up a phrasal or idiomatic construction expecting an “in”‐complement. In other words, it’s detecting lexical items (verbs, adjectives, etc.) that “call for” a following “in” (or similar prepositional input) as part of a fixed or semi‐fixed multiword expression.

It’s a signal that the context is forming a hyphenated (or “un‐”) compound modifier—i.e. the model is “seeing” a word like well, most, or un that’s about to be joined (via a hyphen or split token) to produce a common compound adjective or similar expression, which shifts the next-token prediction accordingly.

It appears to be a “linking‐token” feature – a neuron whose burst signals that the current word or subword is being used as a grammatical or compositional connector (such as a conjunction or a morpheme completing a compound) that is crucial for correctly “bridging” to the next token. Removing it causes the language model to lose that connective cue, leading to incoherent or placeholder next-token predictions.

It appears that this feature is a context‐switch or “query‐response” signal. When active it indicates that the preceding text is a user question (or similar prompt), so the model should transition into a proper, well–segmented answer. In its absence the predicted continuation becomes a garbled fragment (e.g. “cknowled”) because the model loses that cue for the correct answer–initiation token boundary.

It appears that this feature “fires” on tokens that serve as markers for typographic or formatting artifacts—often non‐standard (or “glitched”) punctuation/dash characters inserted when text is copied, styled, or comes from mixed‐script sources. In short, the feature detects and signals a stylized, nonstandard punctuation element (often replacing a plain dash or hyphen) that the model then uses to bias its next‐token prediction.

It appears to be a “quantification‐/range marker” – a signal that the upcoming noun phrase will denote a large, diverse, or extensive group (expressed via phrases such as “a whole host,” “a large number,” “a wide range,” etc.).

explanations.explanation: It appears that this feature flags when the model is handling a subword‐boundary in a compound or hyphenated token. In other words, it signals that the current token is the first (or a connecting) piece of a multi‐part word, which then alters the next token’s prediction (e.g. completing “res” to “respected” or “2‐” to “2‐inch”) rather than defaulting to a common, unrelated continuation.

It appears to be a feature that signals a sentence‐ or clause–ending boundary—activating when the context calls for a strong terminal punctuation (like a period, question mark, or exclamation) rather than a milder separator such as a comma.

It appears the feature is effectively “flagging” personal, first‐person self-reference—that is, it signals the presence of an “I” perspective, marking text as expressing personal views, experiences, or agency. This alters subsequent predictions to carry a more subjective, self‐involved tone, whereas when the feature is removed, the model produces a more neutral continuation.
